---
title: "Counterbalancing"
---

Suppose a sentence has a grammatical version and an ungrammatical version. Showing both versions of the same sentence to one participant may reveal the manipulation. Showing only one version avoids that repetition, but it creates a second problem: if every participant sees item A only in the grammatical condition, any special property of item A is inseparable from grammaticality.

[**Counterbalancing**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/) distributes item versions across stimulus lists so that each participant sees an item only once, while each item occurs in every condition across participants. It solves the item condition confound at the level of the complete design.

## Represent the design as a condition map

Let $C_{jl}$ denote the condition assigned to item $j$ in list $l$. For a two condition design with two lists, a complete counterbalance requires

$$
\{C_{j1},C_{j2}\}=\{0,1\}
$$

for every item $j$. Each item must appear once in condition 0 and once in condition 1 across the two lists. Within each list, condition counts should also be balanced so that a participant encounters both conditions equally often.

This requirement is about the mapping from items to lists. Participant assignment to lists is a separate draw governed by the [random assignment mechanism](random-assignment.qmd) introduced earlier.

## Build a two list design by hand

Consider four sentence items and two conditions.

| item | list 1 | list 2 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | grammatical | ungrammatical |
| B | ungrammatical | grammatical |
| C | grammatical | ungrammatical |
| D | ungrammatical | grammatical |

Read the table in two directions. Down list 1, there are two grammatical and two ungrammatical items. The same is true of list 2. Across the row for item A, both conditions occur. The same is true for B, C, and D.

This structure separates item identity from condition. If item A is unusually easy, its ease contributes to the grammatical condition in list 1 and the ungrammatical condition in list 2. Item A cannot explain a condition difference that persists across lists.

The condition map can be generated and checked in R.

```{r}
counterbalance <- data.frame(
  item = rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 2),
  list = rep(c("list_1", "list_2"), times = 4),
  condition = c(
    "grammatical", "ungrammatical",
    "ungrammatical", "grammatical",
    "grammatical", "ungrammatical",
    "ungrammatical", "grammatical"
  )
)

with(counterbalance, table(item, condition))
with(counterbalance, table(list, condition))
```

The first table checks that every item appears in both conditions across lists. The second checks that each list contains equal condition counts. These are different margins of the design, and both matter.

## Lists must reach participants by design

A valid condition map can still be undermined by how lists are distributed. Suppose list 1 is used during the first week and list 2 during the second. Testing week, recruitment source, or experimenter experience may then become associated with list. Because item conditions change with list, those properties may also become associated with condition.

Participants should thus be randomly assigned to lists or assigned through a recorded restricted mechanism that balances list counts. The realized assignment should be checked after missed sessions and exclusions. Planned balance does not imply realized balance.

## Counterbalancing does not remove dependence

Each participant still supplies several responses, and each item is still observed from several participants. Counterbalancing makes the item condition contrast available. It does not make the rows independent or eliminate participant and item variation.

This distinction matters because averaging over a perfectly balanced table can hide heterogeneous effects. An item may respond differently to the manipulation, and a participant may be more sensitive to the contrast. The [random slope models introduced earlier](../regression-models/random-slopes.qmd) can represent variation in the condition contrast across repeated units, but the model still depends on the counterbalanced design for an interpretable comparison.

## More than two factors

Several factors can require more lists. If two binary manipulations are fully crossed, each item has four possible versions. A complete design distributes all four versions across lists while showing only one version of an item to each participant.

Using only part of the crossing is possible, but omitted combinations impose assumptions about which effects can be separated. Before collection, write the item by list condition map and verify that every planned contrast changes within items across the complete design. This check is more informative than relying on a label such as Latin square without inspecting the actual assignments.

## Check balance after data collection

A design can be balanced in its plan but unbalanced in its collected observations. Missing sessions, programming errors, or unequal exclusions can produce this discrepancy. After collection, tabulate item by condition, list by condition, and participant by condition using the retained observations.

A second failure occurs when a condition is permanently attached to an item. No amount of participant balance can then distinguish the condition effect from the item. This failure must be repaired in the stimulus lists, not in the fitted model.

::: {.callout-note title="Audit the counterbalance"}
1. Which table margin checks that every item appears in every condition?
2. Which table margin checks that a participant assigned to one list encounters balanced condition counts?
3. Why can assigning list 1 before list 2 confound list with testing time?
4. Does perfect counterbalancing make repeated responses independent?
:::

## Summing up

Counterbalancing distributes item versions so that condition can vary within items across the complete design without repeating an item within a participant. The realized data must preserve both the item margin and the list margin. The next page asks which realized observations remain after applying [exclusion rules](exclusion-rules.qmd).
